newsitem.title: JAPAN: Residents of Okinawa go to polls over U.S. bases.
newsitem.headline: Residents of Okinawa go to polls over U.S. bases.

text.p: Residents of Okinawa voted in a referendum on Sunday on whether the huge U.S. military presence on the southern Japanese island should be reduced.
No problems were reported at the 302 polling stations across the island, which opened at 7 a.m. (2200 GMT Saturday) and were to close at 6 p.m. (0900 GMT). There are 900,000 eligible voters.
The referendum, the nation's first on any subject, gives residents a chance to vent years of frustration over the concentration of U.S. military forces on the island.
It is expected to deliver a resounding vote in favour of streamlining the U.S. presence. Only a few ultra-nationalists have been against the idea.
Okinawa Governor Masahide Ota, who wants all U.S. forces removed, cast his ballot early in the morning at the provincial capital of Naha.
"This is a historic moment because it is the first time that Okinawa residents are able to express their will over the military bases, which were more or less forced upon us," he said.
Although the result is not legally binding, strong support for cutbacks would help Ota's drive to continue demanding the central government streamline U.S. bases on the island.
Okinawa holds 75 percent of all U.S. military bases in Japan, representing about half of the 47,000 U.S. military personnel in the country.
The debate has also become a major political problem for Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto.
He has indicated that the result of the Okinawa vote is a major factor in his decision on whether or not to call early general elections.
The long-simmering anger over the bases flared up last September after the rape of an Okinawan schoolgirl by three U.S. servicemen.
Japan has never held a referendum and none of the country's 47 prefectures have ever held a provincial one, over any issue.
